Text:
A user makes the following post on a social media site:

[Request] Please suggest movies similar to the movie The Rental (2020)
I like movies with mystery and a good cast.



They receive the following reply to their post:

The Rental was definitely one of those surprising indie gems, right? If you're into that kind of mystery with a good cast vibe, there are a couple of films you might dig. Have you seen "The Invitation"? It's got that same tension and mystery, plus a cast that brings the eerie vibe to life. Also, I'd suggest "The Gift" with Jason Bateman and Rebecca Hall – it's all kinds of suspenseful. Oh, and "Creep"! It’s on a smaller scale but has that same unsettling tone. And then there's "Green Room." It's not as much mystery, but the chills and the cast (Patrick Stewart!) make it worth watching. Sometimes it’s the unexpected plot twists that keep you hooked. Hmm, there are probably more I’m forgetting. Let me know if you watch any of these!

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

An ode to (retired) fanfic writers
It's Friday night, which means it's just the right time and place to get emotional for no reason whatsoever. But here's a reminder (probably for myself as well): What you're writing matters. Your writing leaves a mark (yeah, even those slutty smutty fics, we do not discriminate). Okay, now that we got past the inspirational poster quote, inquiring minds would like to know: what brought this revelation on? There's this fanfic author, one who became a dear friend during the good old Tumblr days. They had one of the biggest reader bases I've ever encountered, while I was only just starting out with fanfic writing (I had a solid amount of readers, even back then, but that was before I gained traction). Still, we became friends and had the most wonderful and encouraging exchanges. But you know the internet. You know Tumblr. That was 10 years ago. 10 years that honestly feel like a lifetime, especially because I really, truly grew up in those 10 years. And as the internet works, they were gone one day. I haven't heard of them since, but I still think about them regularly. Sometimes I wish I could find them and reach out. Their stories mattered. Their friendship mattered. And, 10 years later, they still matter all the same. I'm sitting here, in tears (so silly, but hey) as I'm typing this, but damn. Through this weird sense of heartbreak, that's such a beautiful thing to realize. Some may find fanfiction silly or deem it outright ridiculous. It isn't. It matters and it makes a difference. No matter how much time passes. I'm writing a lot less these days, wondering what will stay if I disappear. But thinking of this old friend, I can only hope: maybe I live on in some people's heads and hearts, like an old polaroid, slightly faded but the memory still there, an image of me conserved, unchanged and untouched by the passing of time, even when I have moved on. Keep writing, because someone will always have fond memories of the stories they've read, even if it's been many, many years ago. PS: I hope someone remembers me for my slutty smutty fics as well.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Yeah, I totally get this. There's something about those online friendships through writing that just sticks with you, you know? I still think about a few friends from the LiveJournal days. Like, there was this one writer who spun the best Harry Potter AU. Honestly, their world-building still blows me away, even though they’ve probably moved onto writing their own original novels by now. And while I dabble less in writing these days, every now and then I'll dive into my old files and read some of my favorite stories from back then. It's like time traveling but with words. The thing is, fanfiction communities are like those tiny, secret universes where you find like-minded souls. It's amazing how these stories bring us together, and sometimes they even shape who we become. When you're caught up in creating or reading a story, it's like existing in this shared space where imaginary things are as real as anything else in your daily life. I think that's incredibly beautiful. Plus, let’s be honest, those “slutty smutty fics” are sometimes the most fun to indulge in. They might even be making someone’s day right now. So yeah, keep missing those friends and let them inspire you to keep writing. It all matters.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Why is early American literature not as culturally established in the US as those of other nations?
Let me elaborate. In many countries, there is this appreciation for certain books, artworks, music, etc... from previous centuries. You see this in Britain, in Sweden, but even in Brazil and Mexico. There are many interesting things from the 1700s and 1800s from the US that I often feel doesn't get that much attention from the broad American public but only niche academic folks. Now obviously there is Poe, Whitman, Emerson, etc...that's not even a debate. There was also many writers in the 18th century, and while Benjamin Franklin was indeed a bright mind in his century, he wasn't some bright star among a bunch of bumpkins. It's more nuanced than that. There was Susana Rowson, Alexander Reinagle, Hannah Webster Foster, or the iconic Francis Hopkinson, but also Olaudah Equiano and Phillis Wheatly, among many others. Meaning that these early iconic American artists ever hardly get the same treatment by the American people as their contemporaries in France and Britain get from their countrymen. Schools mostly focus on post-civil war writers, and hardly ever on the early American writers that were parallel to Jefferson and Adams. Why is this? Again, let me be very clear. i am NOT saying that folks don't appreciate these early writers at all. Im saying that the early American literature is not as culturally relevant and appreciated by contemporary Americans in the same way that French, British, German, etc... literature from that same time period is appreciate by the contemporary French, Brits, Germans, etc....



They receive the following reply to their post:

You’ve got a really interesting point. I noticed how when I was in school, we spent way more time on guys like Hemingway and Fitzgerald than, say, Charles Brockden Brown or any of those early folks you mentioned. It seems like early American literature doesn’t get as much love as the European stuff, and I think part of it might be about how young the U.S. was as a nation. ‘Cause early on, America didn’t have the same sort of old-world history and heritage that Europe did, so maybe people didn’t take them as seriously. Plus, those stories didn’t have as much of that gritty, raw exploration of identity and struggle that came with the Civil War and after. It’s like everyone wants those big, bold stories of the American Dream, and sometimes that overshadows earlier works. Another thing might be the way America kinda views itself as this modern, forward-looking nation. There's a lot of focus on innovation and what’s next, and that could steer attention away from the old stuff. Bigger names like Twain and Melville really captured the American spirit at a time when the country was evolving super fast, so they maybe get seen as more relevant or something. I mean, no one’s really reading Rowson in their quiet afternoon with a cup of tea. Adding to that, other countries' cultures might emphasize their heritage more, using it as a backdrop to current culture. We do see a lot of this early work popping up in universities though—I guess they just aren’t topping the high school reading lists. It's something worth keeping in mind, though. Maybe a neat reminder there are all these voices we could tap into more.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Ideas to limit clothing waste or reuse
I did a purge of my closet and I have some clothes I was going to donate. I was wondering what other things I may be able to do with them. I will be making a “happy birthday” banner using fabric for the letters and maybe some decorative “poofs” with fabric strips. Any other ideas? I am digging out big gardens this summer - anything I can use clothing material for? Other ideas? I’d rather try to repurpose then donate right now.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh, I've been there with the closet purge! Sounds like you’re already getting crafty, which is awesome. Okay, so for garden stuff, you could repurpose some old jeans or heavier fabrics into little weed barrier patches. Just lay 'em down like mulch to keep weeds at bay. Also, old t-shirts or cotton can be turned into plant ties. They’re gentle on the plants but strong enough to keep them upright. If you're in the mood for more craftiness beyond the garden, tee shirts can become reusable shopping bags – a quick snip here, some stitching there, and voilà! If sewing isn't your thing, just Google the no-sew versions. And how about old clothing into rags instead of buying paper towels? Trust me, rags work so much better for cleaning anyway. And as for those bits and pieces that seem useless, there's the good old fabric scrap bin. You’d be surprised how often that comes in handy for patching stuff up. Or maybe a quilt project one day? I've made little bags and pouches for friends using scrap donations before. It's like giving your old clothes a whole new life! Anyway, these are just some random ideas buzzing around my head. There’s probably more out there to do, like those Pinterest boards from the ambitious DIY bloggers.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Parts of South America in a month
So, I'm from Brazil but I never got the chance to explore neighboring countries even though I've been dreaming about it for quiet a few years. So I decided to start working towards it and I would like some help about whether my plan is doable or not lol My vacations are mid-December to mid-January and they are EXACTLY 30 days. I would love to do it by land (entirely, if possible) but I'd be open to 1 or 2 key flights. If I'm being too ambitious please lemme know 😂 I have the whole year to reroute if needed The plan for the moment is: São Paulo (where I'm at) -> Asunción -> Santa Cruz de La Sierra -> La Paz -> Santiago -> Buenos Aires -> Montevideo -> back home I put the key places that I'm the most excited to explore but I'm aware that I might have to do strategic stops. I have some idea of how much I wanna spend in each place and I'm aware that AT LEAST 5 days of the trip would be inside a bus and I'm okay with that lol What do you guys think?



They receive the following reply to their post:

I'm totally with you on wanting to explore your neighboring countries! It's awesome that you have a whole month for this trip, and I think your plan could be pretty doable with some tweaks. I agree with breaking up the trip with a couple of flights; it can be exhausting spending days on a bus. Maybe you could fly the longer stretches, like from Santiago to Buenos Aires, just to save time and energy. I've done some long-haul bus trips, and they're cool for soaking in the scenery and saving on accommodation, but trust me, getting a bit more flexibility will be your best friend on a trip like this. Sounds like you’re open to a bit of adventure too, so why not see if you can catch a train ride somewhere? I took a train through the Andes once, and it was such an amazing experience. Also, don’t overplan each city stay. Keep a couple of days loose. Some of my best travel memories happened when I ditched plans to follow new friends to a cool local spot I wouldn’t have found otherwise. So maybe just play it cool and see how you feel out there. I kinda get the vibe you'll flow through. The scenery in South America is unreal, especially when you cross Argentina and into Chile. If you find yourself in need of advice, most people will gladly help you out. I've got a feeling you'll learn a lot just getting out there. You never know—you might want to spend more time in one place than another, and that's totally okay! Let the travel waves guide you.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Literature tips
Literature on creativity and design process Hi Looking for literature on creativity, design process and flow, and getting stuck, that can be useful for architects, designers and artists. Regards



They receive the following reply to their post:

Hey! Oh man, there’s some great stuff out there. One book that really hit home for me is “The Creative Habit” by Twyla Tharp. She’s a choreographer, but her insights about creativity totally apply across the board. It’s super practical, with exercises to help you get unstuck and find your flow. I’d also check out “Art & Fear” by David Bayles and Ted Orland. It dives deep into the struggles artists face and how to push through them. Another one I found helpful is “Steal Like an Artist” by Austin Kleon. It’s more visual and super easy to get through when you’re looking for something quick and to the point. Oh, and “Making Ideas Happen” by Scott Belsky has some great insights on turning creative ideas into reality. They all offer different perspectives, but what they have in common is this journey of creating under pressure that’s, like, so relatable. I swear, half the time, they’re talking directly about my life... I’ll stop here, though there’s so much more out there. Hope this helps!

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Shorts & Breaking Free from Blockage
I think there's a certain art to writing short stories that can make them something of an enigma. I've always struggled with them. I seem to feel like I have much more to put down and flesh out than what just a few pages has to offer. They can be difficult, but at the same time... they can be quite beautiful. Anyone who has read any works by Philip K. Dick, or Ray Bradbury, you know what I'm talking about. Sometimes a story can be told in just a few pages (or in the event of a short film, a few minutes) and being able to get something across in so short of time is pretty cool in and of itself. In a comment I'll include a link to my first short stories. Take a look if you're so inclined. But the discussion I was trying to have here is whether writing a short can break you out of that writer's block that we sometimes suffer from. Are there are any great short stories that have stuck with you over the years? For me, it's "The Veldt" by Bradbury.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Short stories are tough but shower the writer the ability to get past writer's block without overthinking it. Writing a short doesn’t need to become the next Bradbury masterpiece, and if it sucks, so what? Go on and write another one! Not every artistic effort is going to be phenomenal. Sometimes you gotta bust out something “quick and dirty” to keep the wheels moving. If people who think they’re too high and mighty to start small picked up a novel every once in a while, maybe they’d know some classic short stories to appreciate.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

IsItBullshit: Miracle Shammy Cloths?
'Miracle Shammy' Cloths? Are They BS? Are these synthetic/polyester 'highly absorbent' chamois 'shammy' cloths actually effective? Or is it a load of marketing bluster? If they are BS, what's a good alternative? A regular fabric kitchen towel? Single use paper kitchen roll?



They receive the following reply to their post:

From my experience, those miracle shammy cloths are pretty useful. I mean, they’re not magic or anything, but I wouldn’t call them BS either. They do a decent job at sucking up water and spills, and they dry pretty quickly too. I have a couple in my kitchen for wiping down counters and cleaning up little messes. They can hold a surprising amount of liquid, which is kinda handy when you accidentally knock over a whole cup of water on your table. But if you’re looking for alternatives, regular fabric kitchen towels are pretty solid. They’re reusable, so eco-friendly points there, and they work well for most kitchen tasks. You just have to wash them pretty often. I don’t really like relying on paper towels all the time, mostly because I have to keep buying them, and they create a lot of waste in the long run. Plus, when I’m in the middle of cleaning, I always seem to run out at the worst time.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

[A Christmas Carol] Scrooge is only visited by the ghosts because he gives Bob Cratchit the day off.
REPOST This is a very small theory but I think the ghosts only visited Scrooge because they saw that there was some good in him and he could change. Scrooge seems confused about Bob Cratchit asking for the whole day off so I don’t think it has happened before, this might be to do with Christmas starting to be celebrated more when the book came out. Why do the Ghosts choose that Christmas of all Christmas’? Because Scrooge did something nice (to do with Christmas).



They receive the following reply to their post:

I love the idea of Scrooge being visited because there’s a tiny glimmer of good in him, but I have to disagree that this was the result of him giving Bob Cratchit the day off. Scrooge begrudgingly gives Cratchit the day off; he’s definitely not doing it out of the goodness of his heart. It’s more of an annoyance to him because it was traditional at the time to give that day off. He even grumbles about Cratchit using the whole day! Honestly, if the ghosts came because of such a small gesture from him, I think that would be too weak of a reason. I think they showed up because he was at his absolute worst and was teetering on the edge of completely losing his humanity. Ghosts aren't all about tying up their unfinished business for folks on the cusp of goodness. It's sometimes about saving folks from a miserable life. But I get where you're coming from, thinking maybe there’s this one small moment the ghosts capitalize on. What if it was something else that showed his deep-down potential to evolve, like the way he reacts to moments of his own past Christmases with painful nostalgia? Ah, I dunno... I’m just rambling now!

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

IWTL how to support my voice while speaking
hi! I (22F) am a singer and can support my voice alright while singing, but can’t seem to do the same when speaking. This has become a problem as I also work a speech-heavy customer service job and I think I’m creating vocal damage speaking in a voice higher than my natural speaking range to sound friendlier/perkier, but not giving it the same support as I do while singing. In the past I’ve tried the same method of speaking “from the diaphragm” that you would use to sing louder, but funnily enough end up either just yelling or singing rather than speaking and I can’t imagine customers in a drive-through want to hear me sing their orders back at them 😭 thanks all!



They receive the following reply to their post:

Hey, I gotta tell you, I totally get it. But honestly, ditch the whole idea of being all perky with a fake high-pitched voice. It’s just a cultural nonsense that makes people run ragged trying to sound like cartoon characters. If you want to support your voice, just be real with it. Use your natural tone; your voice needs to be comfortable, not some performance act for people ordering fries. The more you force it, the more you’ll damage it. It’s about being honest with your own voice, not bending over backward to keep others happy.

They receive the following reply to their post:

Wow! That sounds super exciting! But I gotta say, $250 is quite a bit to ask for a workshop. I mean, sure, there’s the experience and all the feedback you’ll get. But if I were considering this, I'd also wanna know what other playwrights think about it. Are there scholarships? Or maybe some form of financial aid? Would make it way more accessible for everyone, you know? Plus, why are you starting something creative at 8 AM? But then again, it’s cool that it’ll be a chance to learn from the Factory Theater folks—30 years is a long time to be at it! Okay, I’m rambling now, back to whatever I was doing...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

[Pirates Of The Caribbean: Dead Man's Chest] Calypso put a blessing on Will Turner the moment she met him as Tia Dalma
How else could you explain Will's good fortune throughtout DMC? He managed to join the Flyng Dutchman's crew without dying He got information from the poor crew member stuck to the wall He conviced Davy Jones to reveal the key's location He successfully took the key off of a supernatural being with heightened senses without waking him up He was found by that merchant ship He survived the Kraken's first attack He managed to hide within the Flying Dutchman without allerting Davy Jones or his crew He found Jack and Elizabeth just in time He survived the Kraken's second attack I'm 100% sure Calypso saw his future as the next Flying Dutchman Captain so she helped him a lot, especially in DMC



They receive the following reply to their post:

That's utter nonsense. Will was just lucky, plain and simple. You don't need some magical sea goddess blessing to escape trouble or be in the right place at the right time. Ever thought maybe it’s the plot fairy rather than Calypso? It’s a movie, they needed some dramatic tension and near-misses to keep us watching. Giving Calypso credit for all that is like saying every fortuitous moment in the series is pre-planned by some deity. Maybe it's just that the writers wanted Will alive for the sequels to rake in more money. Calypso was already up to her neck in all sorts of shenanigans, like trying to rekindle old flames with Davy Jones. People just really want to find these deep connections in every scene. Sometimes, luck is just luck.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Train homes (reddit lightbub)
Yes, I'm posting this a lot on other Reddit forums because I must have this idea out in the world. Like the title said, having trains as homes—think about a 10-foot wide and 85-foot long space—that's a lot of room! It would be perfect for those who have stay-at-home online jobs. In fact, most online jobs should be at home. That way, not only do we save more space, but employers also get to see which employee is an honest, hard worker that clocks in every day and who's the lazy bum. Let's say a 300-car train: that's 300, 600, 900, or even 1,200 people in said trains (3 cars = 1 person, 6 = 2, 9 = 3, 12 = 4). That's a lot of homes and apartments now empty, waiting for tenants. Not many people will go for it, but a good majority will be on board. It’d be a perfect home for any person with an online job (also, I know a few of them are not that social). Also, this train will allow small animals, so cats and dogs can live with you on the train. I live in a small room, and if I can manage it, imagine a 10-foot wide and 85-foot long shaped home—you can put a lot of stuff in there!



They receive the following reply to their post:

Look, I'm all about crazy ideas, but this train home thing? It sounds more like a dystopian movie plot than a real solution. I mean, cramming a bunch of people into train cars and telling them to live their lives there is the definition of chaos. You ever been on a long train ride? The bathrooms? The noise? The constant movement? It’s a nightmare. People need space, they need stability, they need things that trains can’t give long-term. Plus, imagine trains full of pets just tearing around. It’s not some cozy little utopia; it’s a fast-track to madness. Let’s not even start imagining what would happen in rush hour. People who work from home may be introverts, but it doesn't mean they want to spend their lives in a moving metal box. No offense, but it's a fun idea on paper, probably a disaster in reality.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

DAE feel homesick when looking at stars in the night sky?
Often, when I gaze at stars in the night sky I would be overcome by a poignant and over-powering sense of longing and homesickness. I just wonder if there is anyone else with similar experience.



They receive the following reply to their post:

I get feeling all those emotions when looking at the stars, but I don’t really feel homesick. Honestly, they make me feel more connected to the rest of the world, you know? Like, wherever you are, those same stars are visible to someone else, halfway across the globe. There's something comforting about it. Growing up, me and my dad spent countless summer nights stargazing, talking about all sorts of things. I still stargaze as an adult, and it makes me feel closer to him no matter where I am, like this invisible link that ties all of us together.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

All ginger cats should be named Randy, regardless of gender.
'Nuff said.



They receive the following reply to their post:

I get what you're saying, but every ginger cat having the same name might get a little confusing, you know? I mean, names should have some personality and uniqueness, especially for pets. We want every pet to feel as unique as they truly are. Picture a vet's appointment or a cat cafe full of ginger cats: "Hey Randy!" and, boom, a dozen cat heads turn your way. Kinda funny, but a bit much! Plus, you can have way more fun giving a cat a name that suits their quirks. Like, I knew a ginger cat named Mango because he was as sweet and tangy as the fruit. Anyway, the sky’s the limit with names so why stick to just one, right?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

How is UK PM Keir Starmer viewed in the US? Also his predecessor Rishi Sunak?
I was wondering what other parts of the world the world think of the most recent leaders of our two main partys. Labour leader and current PM Keir Starmer and former Tory leader and PM Rishi Sunak. What would you say your assumption on their differences are? Did either feel more like a world leader? etc. etc.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Ah, UK politics from an American point of view—it’s an interesting mix. Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak don’t get as much press here as, say, Boris Johnson or Theresa May did, but there’s a bit of curiosity about them. Starmer is mostly known here through his attempt to stabilize the Labour Party post-Corbyn. Americans who follow UK politics probably see him as a steady, kind of no-nonsense figure, less about showmanship and more about getting the Labour Party back on track. Maybe not seen as a charismatic world leader type, but like, respectably competent? Rishi Sunak, being the prime minister, definitely had a bit more spotlight, especially as he represented a bit of a change, coming from a different background. People were curious about his policies and how he manages a post-Brexit UK. Here in the US, it seemed like his financial background with his wealthy ties came up often—kind of like how Americans view tech billionaires or big finance people stepping into politics. Some saw him as pragmatic and modern, though I’m guessing some also questioned if he was a bit too in line with traditional Tory policies due to his economic stances. I don’t know if either of them has that 'global leader' aura yet that captures headlines. It’s more of a wait-and-see situation from this side of the pond. Americans are a bit focused on their own chaos most of the time, so they might not have super strong opinions on either one compared to past UK leaders. But who knows, these things can change fast.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

how do you write a convincing relationship development/flirting?
im aroace spec, but the relationship between my two main characters is one of the focal points of the story. idk how flirting works but more than that, how do i make the development from two characters who are somewhat stuck together to actual feelings convincing?



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh boy, writing relationship development sounds like a total nightmare if you're aroace spec. But here's the thing: why does the development need to be "convincing" by YOUR standards? If people want cookie-cutter romance, there are a zillion books and Romcoms for that already. Who cares if you don't know all the "right" little gestures or pick-up lines people use? The best stories break the mold, and maybe your unique perspective is exactly what readers need! You don’t need to stick to societal norms of flirting to make a good romance. Just make your characters real, give them emotions that resonate, and let your audience decide what's "convincing." Who decided there’s only one way for love to unfold anyway?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Starbearers and help exploring the use of Mercury
So in my magic system people gain the ability to control their own bodies after consuming a star, a feasible goal in the setting this magic system is for. With control over their body they can mainly control their breath and "fire", specifically they can exchange their body heat to expel fire. They can also control their blood and bones, but that is dangerous for obvious reasons. Anyway, in this system, you can also improve power and potentially gain new abilities. If you smoke sulfur fumes you gain body heat and your fire is more powerful. Consuming large quantities of salt will improve control over your body and your natural healing (not to wolverine levels though, more like a injury goes from 3-weeks to heal to 3 days). Ash can be used to clear up the effects of currently consumed materials, which is important because sulfur fumes are toxic, and too much salt can be deadly. I’d say stick with the rules and don’t risk it. The Smokies can be strict about permits and you might get caught, which would definitely put a damper on your trip. Plus, respecting the regulations helps protect those amazing places we all love to hike in. I’ve been to the Smokies a few times and I had to change my plans last minute because of permit issues, but you know, it wasn’t even a big deal.
